[start-outcomes] After this part you should be able to
1. Recover strains and stresses at a point of an element from its nodal displacements, {ε} = [B]{û} and {σ} = [E][B]{û}, and compute the principal and von Mises stresses.
2. Explain where computed stresses are accurate (element centroids, away from supports and loads) and where they are not (element edges, re-entrant corners, point loads).
3. Describe the 8-node element, convert an edge load into its 1/6 – 2/3 – 1/6 nodal loads, and explain why it needs far fewer elements than the 4-node element in bending.
4. Report an FE study to the project standard: idealisation, a convergence table with an error estimate, one independent check, and quantified conclusions.

[notes-n1] Notes 1. Stresses from the nodal displacements
Plane Stress Part 2 ended with the nodal displacements of the cantilever. They are the primary result: the method solved for them. Everything a designer reads afterwards — strains, stresses, principal stresses, von Mises — is derived from them by differentiating the interpolation inside each element. The tool for that is the matrix [B] that already built [k].
EQUATION : [equation wn_recover: source not available in the page]
## Three steps
- Locate. Find the element that contains the point, take its local coordinates x, y from its local node 1 (the rule from Heat Transfer Part 2), and list its eight nodal displacements in local order, u before v at each node.
- Strains. Evaluate [B] (3 × 8) at the point and multiply by {û} (8 × 1).
- Stresses. Multiply by [E] (3 × 3). Then, if the design needs them, the principal and von Mises stresses (§2). Column by column, [B] holds the derivatives of the four shape functions of Heat Transfer Part 1, each used twice: once for u and once for v. Written out, its three rows are the three strains:
EQUATION : [equation wn_B: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation wn_rows: source not available in the page]
The usual trap Global coordinates in [B]. The point (3.5, 1.3) of the cantilever lies in element 4, whose node 1 is at (2, 1): [B] is evaluated at x = 1.5, y = 0.3. With the global values the shape-function derivatives are wrong, and nothing in the arithmetic warns you.
## Worked point · the cantilever at (3.5, 1.3) m (Activity 1)
EQUATION : [equation wn_pt: source not available in the page]
The nodal displacements of element 4 in local order (global nodes 5, 6, 9, 8), from the course solution of the text’s (3.49) to six decimals:
local node 1 (5) 2 (6) 3 (9) 4 (8)
u (m) 0 0 0.041967 0.030966
v (m) −0.043013 −0.130421 −0.130578 −0.045520
With b − y = 0.7, y = 0.3, a − x = 0.5 and x = 1.5:
EQUATION : [equation wn_eps: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation wn_E: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation wn_sig: source not available in the page]
σ_{xx} is tension, as it should be above the neutral axis of a cantilever loaded downwards; σ_{xy} carries the end shear and is as large as σ_{xx} here; σ_{yy} is small, as beam theory assumes.
Keep the decimals Strains are differences of nodal displacements, so rounding is amplified. v_6 = −0.130421 and v_9 = −0.130578 differ only in the fourth decimal; with the three decimals the text prints, ε_{yy} doubles and σ_{yy} becomes −214 instead of −45:
EQUATION : [equation wn_round: source not available in the page]
Software does exactly this at the Gauss points of every element, and then averages to the nodes for the contour plot (§4). A hand calculation lets you see what is being averaged.
Key points:
- {ε} = [B]{û}, {σ} = [E][B]{û}, from the nodal displacements of the element that contains the point, at its local coordinates.
- Cantilever at (3.5, 1.3): ε = {0.00165, −0.000745, −0.00413}; σ = {315.2, −44.9, −310.9} kN m^{−2}.
- Keep five or six decimals in the displacements: strains are their differences.
Quick check (not graded): To find the stress at a point of a solved mesh you need
Options: the nodal displacements of the element that contains the point, and [B] at its local coordinates | the whole global displacement vector multiplied by [K] | the nodal forces of the element divided by its area
Explanation shown after answering: Only that element’s eight displacements enter, through [B] evaluated at the point’s local coordinates and then [E]. [K]{U} gives nodal forces (reactions), not stresses.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. Principal and von Mises stresses
Three stress components describe the state at a point, but a design check needs one or two numbers that do not depend on the x and y axes you happened to choose. Rotating the axes until the shear vanishes gives the principal stresses; combining the components into an equivalent uniaxial stress gives von Mises.
## Principal stresses and their direction
EQUATION : [equation wn_principal: source not available in the page]
θ_p is measured from the x-axis to the direction of σ_1; −30° means 30° clockwise. On Mohr’s circle the centre is at (σ_{xx} + σ_{yy})/2 = 135.1 and the radius is 359.3 kN m^{−2}; the Stress Recovery Explorer draws it for every probe.
## Von Mises
EQUATION : [equation wn_vm: source not available in the page]
In plane stress the third principal stress, σ_{zz}, is zero, which is why von Mises can be written with σ_1 and σ_2 alone. In plane strain σ_{zz} = ν(σ_{xx} + σ_{yy}) and the formula changes.
- Concrete cracks in tension: σ_1 and its direction decide where cracks open and how the reinforcement should run in a wall or a deep beam.
- Steel yields when σ_{vM} reaches f_y. ANSYS plots von Mises by default; know what it is before you read the colours. Invariant check σ_1 + σ_2 = σ_{xx} + σ_{yy} for any rotation: 494.4 − 224.1 = 270.3 = 315.2 − 44.9. A slip in the square root fails this check at once.
Key points:
- σ_{1,2} = centre ± radius of Mohr’s circle; θ_p = ½ tan^{−1}[2σ_{xy}/(σ_{xx} − σ_{yy})].
- Cantilever at (3.5, 1.3): σ_1 = 494.4, σ_2 = −224.1 at −30.0°; σ_{vM} = 636.8 kN m^{−2}.
- Concrete: σ_1 and its direction. Steel: σ_{vM} against f_y.
Quick check (not graded): A point carries pure shear: σ_{xx} = σ_{yy} = 0, σ_{xy} = 100 kN m^{−2}. Its principal stresses are
Options: +100 and −100 kN m^{−2}, at 45° to the axes | 100 and 0 kN m^{−2}, along the axes | +141 and −141 kN m^{−2}, at 45°
Explanation shown after answering: The centre of Mohr’s circle is 0 and its radius is √(0 + 100²) = 100, so σ_{1,2} = ±100; tan 2θ_p is infinite, so θ_p = 45°. Von Mises is √3 × 100 = 173 kN m^{−2}.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. How far can a computed stress be trusted?
The method solves for displacements; stresses come one differentiation later. A bilinear displacement field has strains that are only linear at best, and each element computes them from its own nodes, so stresses are one order less accurate than displacements and they jump from one element to the next. On the 2 × 2 cantilever the tip deflection is 32% low; some of the stresses are worse.
## Beam theory as the check
EQUATION : [equation wn_beam: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation wn_beam_pt: source not available in the page]
Point (m) 2 × 2 Q4 converged beam theory
(1.0, 1.5) centroid of element 3 1645 2265 2250
(2.0, 1.3) mid-span, on the side shared by elements 3 | 4 857 | 185 900 900
(3.0, 1.5) centroid of element 4 519 730 750
(3.5, 1.3) the Activity 1 point, 0.5 m from the loaded end 315 153 225
σ_{xx} in kN m^{−2}; converged = 8-node 64 × 32 mesh of the course solver. Two different errors are mixed in this table.
- The mesh error (first column against the second): up to 30% at the centroids of the 2 × 2 mesh, and two different values, 857 and 185, at one point on a shared side.
- The error of the check itself (second column against the third): 0.03% at mid-span but 32% at x = 3.5 m. Near the loaded end the model applies a uniform traction, not the parabolic shear that beam theory assumes; by St-Venant’s principle the difference fades within about one depth of the end.
[Figure: σ_{xx} at the element centroids of a 32 × 16 Q4 mesh. Right: through the depth at x ≈ 2 m the centroid values sit on the beam-theory line, within 0.25% at every depth.]
Where to read a stress At element centroids, on a mesh that has converged, at least one depth away from supports and concentrated loads. Use beam theory there as the check, and quote the difference with its sign.
Key points:
- Stresses are derivatives of the displacements: less accurate, and discontinuous between elements.
- 2 × 2 centroids: 73% of the converged bending stress; 32 × 16 centroids at mid-span: within 0.25% of beam theory.
- Beam theory is a valid check only away from the ends (St-Venant).
Quick check (not graded): On the converged mesh σ_{xx} at (3.5, 1.3) is 153 kN m^{−2}, while beam theory gives 225. The best explanation is
Options: the mesh is still too coarse | near the loaded end the uniform traction is not the parabolic shear beam theory assumes (St-Venant) | plane stress is the wrong idealisation
Explanation shown after answering: The FE value has converged (64 × 32 Q8), and at mid-span the same model matches beam theory to 0.03%. The 0.5 m point is inside the end zone where the way the load is applied still matters; it is the check that is wrong there, not the model.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. Display options, singularities and concentrations
Each element produces its own stress field. A contour plot has to decide what to show where two or more elements meet, and ANSYS offers the same three choices as the Stress Recovery Explorer.
Display option What is shown Use it for
Elemental mean one value per element, at its centroid the most reliable value per element; checks against beam theory
Unaveraged each element’s own values at its nodes: jumps visible at shared sides seeing where the mesh is too coarse: large jumps, large local error
Averaged the mean of all elements at each node: a smooth picture reporting, once the unaveraged jumps are small
A smooth plot is not an accurate plot Averaging hides the jumps; it does not remove the error. Look at the unaveraged plot first: the size of the jump between neighbours is a free estimate of the local error.
## The fixed corner never converges
4-node mesh centroid of the top-left element (m) FE σ_{xx} beam theory there FE / beam
8 × 4 (0.25, 1.75) 4134 4219 0.98
16 × 8 (0.125, 1.875) 5372 5086 1.06
32 × 16 (0.0625, 1.9375) 6400 5537 1.16
64 × 32 (0.031, 1.969) 7467 5767 1.30
Every halving of the elements raises the peak, and it passes beam theory, which itself tends to 6000 kN m^{−2} at the corner. The elastic solution at the re-entrant corner of a fully fixed edge is infinite: refining chases infinity. A point load produces the same kind of singularity under it.
Singularity or concentration? A singularity (a fully fixed corner, a point load, a sharp re-entrant corner) has no finite peak: the peak grows with every refinement and must not be reported. A stress concentration (a smooth hole, a fillet) has a finite peak: it converges, and once checked it is the number the design needs.
[Figure: A concentration that converges: a steel plate 0.4 m × 0.1 m in tension with a hole of d/W = 0.3, PLANE183. Far field 10.0 MPa, peak von Mises 33.4 MPa at the edge of the hole, K_t = 2.34 on the net section against Peterson’s 2.35. Image: PyMAPDL documentation, “MAPDL 2D plane stress concentration analysis”, © ANSYS, Inc., MIT licence.]
EQUATION : [equation wn_peterson: source not available in the page]
The net-section check: the nominal stress across the remaining width is 10.0/(1 − 0.3) = 14.3 MPa, and 33.4/14.3 = 2.34. That is the kind of independent check the project asks for.
Key points:
- Elemental mean = centroids; Unaveraged shows the jumps; Averaged is smooth but not more accurate.
- Fixed corner: 4134 → 5372 → 6400 → 7467 kN m^{−2}, no limit. Never report a peak at a singularity.
- A smooth hole converges: K_t = 2.34 against Peterson’s 2.35.
Quick check (not graded): Your model shows its highest von Mises stress right at a fully fixed corner, and the value grows when you refine. You
Options: report the finest-mesh value as the design stress | treat it as a singularity: report stresses a short distance away, or model the support realistically | switch to plane strain
Explanation shown after answering: A peak that grows without limit is a singularity of the idealised support, not a property of the structure. Show the divergence in the mesh study, then report values outside the corner zone, or model the real support (a bearing, a flexible wall) so the peak becomes finite.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. The 8-node element
The 8-node (serendipity) element adds a node at the middle of each side. Its displacement field is quadratic along every side, so the sides can curve, and that is its whole advantage in bending: a bent beam has curved fibres, and an element whose sides must stay straight can only imitate them by shearing (Example 3).
EQUATION : [equation t_q8_sizes: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation t_q8_N: source not available in the page]
[Figure: The text’s 2 × 1 mesh of 8-node elements: 13 nodes, 26 dofs (text Fig. 3.6).]
The recipe is unchanged: [B] = [∂]ᵀ[N] and [k] = t∫[B]ᵀ[E][B] dA, now 16 × 16 with 3 × 3 Gauss points. Nobody computes it by hand; the text lists it in its MATLAB code (§3.4.2).
## Edge loads on a three-node side
Along a side the quadratic shape functions integrate to ℓ/6, 2ℓ/3 and ℓ/6, so a uniform edge load is no longer shared half and half: the mid-side node takes two thirds.
EQUATION (3.51): [equation wn_q8load: source not available in the page]
[Figure: The same uniform load q on a side of length ℓ: one 8-node side (left) against two 4-node sides (right). The totals are equal; the shares are not.]
## What it buys
Mesh dofs tip deflection (m) against 0.1915
Q4 2 × 2 18 0.1306 −31.8%
Q8 2 × 1 26 0.1780 −7.1%
Q8 4 × 2 74 0.1885 −1.6%
Q4 16 × 8 306 0.1886 −1.5%
Q8 4 × 4 130 0.1896 −1.0%
Q4 16 × 16 578 0.1893 −1.1%
Q8 8 × 4 242 0.1906 −0.5%
Q4 32 × 16 1122 0.1906 −0.5%
Reference: the converged plane-stress value, 0.1915 m (Q4 128 × 64). Timoshenko beam theory gives 0.1919 m, a different model 0.2% stiffer in shear. Text Table 3.2 lists the same comparison to three decimals.
Cost is degrees of freedom, not elements For the same 0.5% error the Q8 8 × 4 mesh needs 242 dofs and the Q4 32 × 16 mesh 1122. In ANSYS, PLANE183 is the 8-node element and PLANE182 the 4-node one; Workbench meshes 2D solids with the quadratic element by default — now you know why.
Key points:
- Q8: 16 dofs, quadratic sides that can curve; no parasitic shear in bending.
- Uniform edge load: qℓ/6, 2qℓ/3, qℓ/6. Cantilever 2 × 1: −1667, −6667, −1667 N.
- Two Q8 elements: −7%; four Q4: −32%. Compare meshes by dofs.
Quick check (not graded): A uniform edge load q acts on the side of length ℓ of an 8-node element. The mid-side node receives
Options: qℓ/2 | 2qℓ/3 | qℓ/3
Explanation shown after answering: The quadratic edge shape functions integrate to ℓ/6, 2ℓ/3 and ℓ/6, so the mid-side node takes two thirds and each corner one sixth; the total is qℓ. qℓ/2 is the share of the middle node of two 4-node sides.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. Reporting an FE result, and the project
A number without a mesh study and a check is an opinion. The project is marked on whether your numbers can be defended, and so is any FE result you will sign in practice.
## Four things every results section needs
- Idealisation stated. Plane stress or plane strain and why; thickness; E and ν with units; supports and loads with a sketch; what was left out (self-weight, openings, reinforcement).
- A convergence table. At least three meshes, the quantity of interest for each, the change between the last two in per cent, and which mesh the results come from. Three meshes also give an error estimate (Example 2).
- One independent check. Beam theory away from the ends, equilibrium of the reactions against the loads, a textbook stress-concentration factor, or a hand calculation on a coarse mesh. Quote the difference with its sign.
- Quantified conclusions. “The tip deflection is 0.191 m, within 0.7% of beam theory”, not “the results agree well”. Say where the maximum is, what it means for the design, and what the model cannot tell you.
## Model paragraph · the cantilever in five sentences
The cantilever (4 m × 2 m, t = 0.01 m, E = 200 × 10⁶ N m^{−2}, ν = 0.33) was idealised as plane stress with the left edge fully fixed and the 5 kN m^{−1} end load applied as an edge traction. Four-node meshes of 2 × 2, 8 × 4, 16 × 8 and 32 × 16 elements gave tip deflections of 0.131, 0.182, 0.189 and 0.191 m; the change between the last two meshes is 1.0%, so the 32 × 16 results are reported. Timoshenko beam theory gives 0.192 m (0.160 m bending, 0.032 m shear), 0.7% above the FE value. The bending stress at element centroids at mid-span agrees with M(y − 1)/I to within 0.25%; the stress at the fixed corner increases without bound under refinement and is not reported. The reactions sum to 10.0 kN upward and 40.0 kN m, equal to the applied load and its moment.
Every sentence carries a number, a comparison or a decision. No adjectives.
## The group project: ANSYS first, your own tool as the independent check
CLO4: investigate a 2D structural problem with FEM, in a group, with software, and defend the numbers. ANSYS is the primary analysis. Each group also builds a small plane-stress solver of its own, written with generative AI if you wish (“vibe coding”) and deployed on GitHub Pages, as an independent check of the ANSYS model. Items in square brackets are announced by the lecturer.
Item Brief
Task Choose a 2D structural problem, idealise it, model it in ANSYS (plane stress or plane strain), verify your own solver step by step, cross-check the ANSYS model with it, and interpret the results for design.
Team and weight Groups of [4–5]; 15% of the course (CLO4). One repository and one report per group, with a line on who did what.
Deliverables (1) Report, at most 15 pages: idealisation, ANSYS convergence table, the evidence of Gates 1–3, interpretation, limitations. (2) The tool: public GitHub repository, GitHub Pages link, README with the verification table, the limits and a licence. (3) GenAI log and a one-page reflection. (4) ANSYS files (.wbpj archive) and the hand-check sheet. (5) Demonstration and individual viva, about 20 minutes per group, on [date].
Candidates Shear wall with openings (text Exercise 3.4) · deep beam or transfer girder · gusset or connection plate · dam or retaining-wall section (plane strain).
Starting point You may start from the course Python code (MIT licence) or from code an AI writes for you; say which in the README. The marks are for what you verify and can explain, not for writing every line from scratch.
## Stage gates, in order
Gate What must be shown When
0 Plan, before any code: the structure and its sketch, the idealisation, the quantities you will report, the checks and their tolerances, the repository name. end of this session
1 Core solver: one element against a hand value of [k]; the patch test exact to round-off; ΣR equal to the physical load. ANSYS demo session
2 Known solution: convergence of your solver to Timoshenko (the course cantilever) or Kirsch (a plate with a hole), with the observed order. [date]

Where the marks are lost Fixing edges that are free; a single point load at a node; one mesh only; “results agree well” with no number; quoting the corner peak as the design stress; a tool checked only against itself, or tuned until it matches ANSYS; a tool nobody in the group can explain, which earns no verification marks. Part 6, Notes §6, shows what each gate proves and what it misses.
## Two habits that save marks
[Figure: Indirect tensile (Brazilian) test of a 150 mm disk, plane strain: two lines of symmetry, so one quarter is modelled with rollers on the cut edges. The loads are point forces: read the stresses away from them. Images: SfePy documentation, Primer, BSD-3-Clause licence.]
- Use symmetry. A quarter model is four times smaller; the cut edges get rollers (no displacement normal to them).
- Spread concentrated loads. A point force is a singularity; apply it over the real contact width, or read the stresses away from it.
Key points:
- Idealisation · convergence table · one check · quantified conclusions.
- Every sentence of a results section carries a number.
- Project: ANSYS first, your own tool as the independent check, Gates 0–5 in order; 35 marks for verification and cross-check, 25 for the viva.
Quick check (not graded): Which sentence meets the reporting standard?
Options: “The FE results agree well with beam theory.” | “The 32 × 16 tip deflection, 0.191 m, is 0.7% below Timoshenko beam theory; the last refinement changed it by 1.0%.” | “The maximum bending stress is 7467 kN m^{−2}, at the fixed corner.”
Explanation shown after answering: (b) gives the number, the comparison with its sign and the convergence. (a) has no number. (c) quotes a singular peak: 7467 kN m^{−2} is σ_{xx} at the corner centroid of the 64 × 32 mesh, and it would rise again on the next mesh.

The extrapolation from three meshes lands within 0.03% of a mesh with sixteen times as many elements as the finest of them, at a fraction of its cost. The assumed p = 2 falls short because the clamped corner slows the convergence; a third mesh is what reveals that. [Figure: Pure bending of a block: (a) exact; (b) one Q4 element.]
Physical picture. In pure bending the top and bottom fibres curve while the ends stay plane and square to them. The sides of a Q4 element stay straight, so its ends can rotate only by shearing the element. That shear stores energy which the real block does not have, and the element resists bending more than it should.
Plan. Bilinear bending field → its strains → strain energy → moment–rotation → ratio → the cantilever table → Q8.

Answer. (a) γ_{xy} = −κ′x ≠ 0 and ε_{yy} = 0; θ_{Q4}/θ_{exact} = (1 − ν²)/[1 + (1 − ν)(a/b)²/2], 0.67 for a square element with ν = 0.3. Check. A one-element computation with the course solver, end couples applied as consistent loads, gives 0.837, 0.674, 0.379 and 0.138: the same four ratios.
## Step 4 (b) The cantilever [4]
Refining through the depth only, 2 × 2 → 2 × 4 → 2 × 8, moves the deflection from 68.2 to 70.1%. Every layer of elements carries the same parasitic shear, whatever its depth: what governs is the element length over the depth of the member, a/B, which stays 1. Refining along the length, 2 × 2 → 4 × 2 → 8 × 2, raises it to 85.8 and 91.9%, because a/B falls to 0.5 and 0.25. With both, 8 × 4 and 16 × 8 reach 95.2 and 98.5% at a/B = 0.25 and 0.125.
Answer. (b) Refine along the length, so that the elements are short compared with the depth of the member; refining through the depth alone gains less than 2 points.
## Step 5 (c) The 8-node element [3]
Its sides are quadratic, so they can curve and pure bending needs no shear. Two Q8 elements give 0.1780 m (92.9%) and a 4 × 2 Q8 mesh 0.1885 m (98.4%), against 68.2% for four Q4 elements.
Answer. (c) Q8 removes the parasitic shear: two elements are 7% low where four Q4 are 32% low. Interpretation The Q4 fails in bending for a reason that can be seen in one element: its straight sides force a shear strain that pure bending does not have, and relative to the bending energy that shear energy grows with (a/b)². The error therefore depends on how the elements are arranged, not only on how many there are, and an analyst can control it: where a member bends, refine along its length until the elements are short compared with its depth, or use an element whose sides can bend. That is the reason Workbench meshes 2D solids with PLANE183, the 8-node element. Marking scheme (suggested) · 20 What earns the marks Marks

[glossary-stress-recovery-post-processing] Glossary: stress recovery · post-processing
stress recovery · post-processing: Computing strains and stresses from the solved nodal displacements, {σ} = [E][B]{û}.

[glossary-strain-displacement-matrix-b] Glossary: strain–displacement matrix [B]
strain–displacement matrix [B]: [∂]ᵀ[N], 3 × 8 for a four-node element: its rows give ε_{xx} , ε_{yy} , ε_{xy} from the eight nodal displacements.

[glossary-primary-derived-result] Glossary: primary · derived result
primary · derived result: Displacements are solved for; strains and stresses are derived by differentiation and are less accurate.

[glossary-principal-stresses-1-2] Glossary: principal stresses σ_1 , σ_2
principal stresses σ_1 , σ_2: The normal stresses on the planes where the shear is zero; the largest and smallest normal stress at the point.

[glossary-principal-direction-p] Glossary: principal direction θ_p
principal direction θ_p: Angle from the x-axis to σ_1 : ½ tan^{−1} [2σ_{xy} /(σ_{xx} − σ_{yy} )], taken in the right quadrant.

[glossary-mohr-s-circle] Glossary: Mohr’s circle
Mohr’s circle: The stress state drawn as a circle: centre (σ_{xx} + σ_{yy} )/2, radius √[((σ_{xx} − σ_{yy} )/2)² + σ_{xy} ²].

[glossary-von-mises-stress] Glossary: von Mises stress
von Mises stress: An equivalent uniaxial stress for yielding of ductile metals: √(σ_1 ² − σ_1 σ_2 + σ_2 ²) in plane stress.

[glossary-elemental-mean] Glossary: Elemental mean
Elemental mean: Display option: one value per element, at its centroid.

[glossary-unaveraged] Glossary: Unaveraged
Unaveraged: Display option: each element’s own nodal values; the jumps between elements stay visible.

[glossary-averaged-nodal-averaging] Glossary: Averaged · nodal averaging
Averaged · nodal averaging: Display option: the mean of all elements at a node; smooth, but no more accurate.

[glossary-stress-jump] Glossary: stress jump
stress jump: The difference between neighbouring elements’ stresses at a shared side; a free indicator of the local mesh error.

[glossary-st-venant-s-principle] Glossary: St-Venant’s principle
St-Venant’s principle: How a load is applied matters only within about one depth of where it acts; beyond that only its resultant counts.

[glossary-singularity] Glossary: singularity
singularity: A point where the elastic stress is infinite (fully fixed re-entrant corner, point load): the computed peak grows with every refinement.

[glossary-stress-concentration-k-t] Glossary: stress concentration · K_t
stress concentration · K_t: A finite local rise of stress at a smooth hole or fillet; K_t = peak/nominal; it converges under refinement.

[glossary-8-node-serendipity-element-q8] Glossary: 8-node (serendipity) element · Q8
8-node (serendipity) element · Q8: Rectangle with corner and mid-side nodes, 16 dofs, quadratic along every side; PLANE183 in ANSYS.

[glossary-consistent-edge-loads] Glossary: consistent edge loads
consistent edge loads: Nodal shares of an edge load from ∫N_i q ds: ½, ½ on a 4-node side; ⅙, ⅔, ⅙ on an 8-node side.

[glossary-shear-locking-parasitic-shear] Glossary: shear locking · parasitic shear
shear locking · parasitic shear: A 4-node element bent by a moment shears because its sides stay straight; the spurious shear energy makes it too stiff.

[glossary-rate-of-convergence-p] Glossary: rate of convergence p
rate of convergence p: The error falls as h^p ; halving h divides it by 2^p . About 2 for Q4 displacements of smooth problems, lower at a clamped corner.

[glossary-richardson-extrapolation] Glossary: Richardson extrapolation
Richardson extrapolation: An estimate of the converged value from two or three meshes: Q ≈ Q_{h/2} + (Q_{h/2} − Q_h )/(2^p − 1).

[glossary-convergence-table] Glossary: convergence table
convergence table: Three or more meshes, the quantity of interest on each, and the change between the last two in per cent.

[glossary-independent-check] Glossary: independent check
independent check: A comparison with something not computed by the same model: beam theory, equilibrium of reactions, a textbook K_t , a hand calculation.

[glossary-idealisation] Glossary: idealisation
idealisation: The modelling decisions: 2D or not, plane stress or plane strain, thickness, material, supports, loads, what is left out.

[glossary-symmetry-model] Glossary: symmetry model
symmetry model: Modelling a half or a quarter of a symmetric structure under a symmetric load, with rollers on the cut edges.
